The federal transport agency moved this afternoon to calm investors after a week of speculation about toll road contracts. In a statement, the agency confirmed that the tariff review for highway concessions will go ahead in October, but clarified that it would follow the formula written into each contract. The agency's director acknowledged that seven operators had filed rebalancing claims after the floods, and said the claims would be assessed individually. She declined to say whether the floods would be treated as force majeure. Market reaction was cautious. One analyst told us that investors had expected a clearer answer on the floods, and warned that uncertainty over the claims could delay two auctions planned for the first half of next year.

Most investors read the tariff clause and the investment schedule, and then they stop. I want to talk about the two clauses they skip. The first is force majeure. People think it is a formality, but in a country with floods and droughts it decides who pays when the road is under water. Read the list of events, and read who has to prove what. The second is the grandfathering clause. When a government changes the rules, this is the sentence that says whether your contract is protected or not. I have seen a fund lose a year of returns because its lawyers assumed the old rules would continue, and the clause said otherwise. None of this is exciting. All of it belongs in your due diligence.
